reason: B keeps a reader inside scenes: the cross-examination is dramatized in actual dialogue, the hemlock death is narrated moment by moment, and Jebel Sahaba gives the evidence discussion a concrete place and body count to argue over. A's Socrates is a competent summary rather than a scene, and its long middle section on the Hayes trial never narrates the case at all - it circles the same abstraction (witnesses held portions, the court turned an injury into a felony) for several paragraphs, and even garbles its own framing with 'a century and a quarter after the death of John Hayes' before dating the murder to 1722. B also moves better: its definitional taxonomy is punctuated by concrete instances and closed by a single deliberate recap, while A stacks undifferentiated definitional paragraphs and then bloats two of its longest paragraphs with merged material that restates points already made.
